source.title: Comparative Efficacy and Safety of Antidiabetic Drug Regimens Added to Metformin Monotherapy in Patients with Type 2 Diabetes: A Network Meta-Analysis
source.source_type: systematic review and network meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
source.scope_note: Secondary-source extraction. Result atoms represent estimates reported by the meta-analysis and are tagged secondary_reported_result; they do not imply that the meta-analysis itself enrolled participants.

extraction.coverage_scope: Source-wide methods, population, headline conclusions, all Table 2 network estimates versus placebo, all reported Table 3 network safety estimates versus placebo, sensitivity/inconsistency findings, limitations, funding, conflicts, and data availability. Full active-vs-active matrix cells in S3–S14 were reconciled for SEA but not individually atomized because doing so would create hundreds of redundant secondary-source estimates beyond the project’s high-value extraction scope.

atoms.canonical_statement: The review assessed comparative efficacy and safety of adjunctive antidiabetic medication therapies in adults with type 2 diabetes inadequately controlled on stable, optimized metformin monotherapy.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: We performed a NMA to assess the comparative efficacy and safety of adjunctive antidiabetic medication therapies in patients with Type 2 DM not adequately controlled on stable and optimized metformin monotherapy.

atoms.canonical_statement: Eligible studies were English-language parallel randomized controlled trials in adults with type 2 diabetes, comparing FDA- or EU-approved antidiabetic adjuncts plus metformin against another adjunct or placebo, with inadequate response to optimized metformin, 12–52 weeks of treatment, and reported change in HbA1c.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: To be included, studies had to: (1) be published in English; (2) utilize a parallel RCT design ... (5) treat patients for 12 to 52 glycemic weeks ... and (6) report change in HbA1c from baseline.

population.label: Adults (≥18 years) with type 2 diabetes inadequately controlled on stable, optimized metformin monotherapy
inclusion_criteria: Adjunctive FDA- or EU-approved antidiabetic therapy plus metformin

atoms.canonical_statement: The network meta-analysis included 62 randomized controlled trials with 32,185 participants evaluating 25 active treatments plus placebo.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: After screening, 62 RCTs (n = 32,185 participants) were included

population.label: Participants in 62 included randomized controlled trials

atoms.canonical_statement: The systematic search covered MEDLINE and Cochrane CENTRAL from database inception through May 2014, supplemented by reference screening, ClinicalTrials.gov, regulatory agency reports, and investigator contact.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: We performed a systematic literature search for all relevant articles from the earliest date through May 2014 in MEDLINE and Cochrane CENTRAL.

atoms.canonical_statement: Two investigators independently reviewed potentially relevant citations.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Two investigators reviewed all potentially relevant citations independently (ESM, CIC).

atoms.canonical_statement: Two investigators independently assessed trial validity using the Cochrane Risk of Bias Tool across seven domains, rating each item low, unclear, or high risk.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Validity assessment was performed by 2 investigators (ESM, DMS) independently using the Cochrane Risk of Bias Tool

atoms.canonical_statement: Two investigators independently extracted data with a standardized tool; disagreements were resolved by discussion or a third investigator.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Two investigators (ESM, DMS) used a standardized tool to independently extract all data with disagreements resolved by discussion or a third investigator (CIC).

atoms.canonical_statement: Efficacy endpoints were changes from baseline in HbA1c, body weight, and systolic blood pressure; safety endpoints were confirmed hypoglycemia, urinary tract infection, and genital tract infection.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Endpoint data collected included mean change from baseline in HbA1c, body weight (BW), and systolic blood pressure (SBP) and the number/proportion of patients experiencing finger stick confirmed hypoglycemia, urinary tract infections (UTIs) and genital tract infections (GTIs).

atoms.canonical_statement: Traditional pairwise meta-analyses used DerSimonian-Laird random-effects models, reporting weighted mean differences for continuous endpoints and relative risks for dichotomous safety endpoints.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: weighted (absolute) mean differences (WMDs) and associated 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated using a DerSimonian and Laird random-effects model

atoms.canonical_statement: When paired variance estimates were unavailable, the authors derived them from available statistics and assumed a baseline-to-final correlation coefficient of 0.5.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: assuming a correlation coefficient of 0.5 between initial and final values

atoms.canonical_statement: Network meta-analysis was performed with netmeta 0.5-0 in R 3.0.2 using a random-effects model with common heterogeneity across comparisons and incorporating direct and indirect evidence.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: We used the package ‘netmeta’ (version 0.5–0) in R (version 3.0.2 ... ) to perform NMA

atoms.canonical_statement: Network inconsistency was assessed by statistically comparing direct and indirect estimates when an indirect estimate could be constructed through a single common comparator.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Inconsistency was assessed by statistically comparing the results from direct and indirect estimates

atoms.canonical_statement: Clinical superiority thresholds were 0.3 percentage points for HbA1c, 2.3 kg for body weight, and 5 mmHg for systolic blood pressure, requiring the lower 95% CI bound to exceed the threshold in the favorable direction.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: We ascribed clinical superiority if one therapy improved HbA1c, BW or SBP by at least 0.3%, 2.3 kg (5 pounds) or 5 mmHg, respectively

atoms.canonical_statement: Sensitivity analyses used 99% confidence intervals to reduce false-positive findings from multiple comparisons.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: we performed sensitivity analyses calculating more conservative 99%CIs.

atoms.canonical_statement: In the network meta-analysis, Acarbose added to metformin changed HbA1c versus placebo by -0.79 percentage points (95% CI -1.09 to -0.48).

atoms.canonical_statement: The review included only English-language randomized controlled trials.
Sparse reporting of urinary and genital tract infections limited the certainty of conclusions for those safety endpoints and raised risk of type II error.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: We found sparse reporting of certain endpoints (UTI and GTI) which makes it difficult to draw concrete conclusions (potential for type 2 error).

atoms.canonical_statement: The network compared 25 active therapies plus placebo across six endpoints, creating a multiple-testing risk of false-positive differences.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: our NMA cross- compared 25 therapies plus placebo on 6 different endpoints; thus multiple hypothesis testing can lead to erred conclusions

atoms.canonical_statement: Limited data and short follow-up prevented assessment of cardiovascular events, pancreatitis, renal dysfunction, and heart failure.

atoms.canonical_statement: Publication bias remained a concern despite the systematic search, backward citation tracking, and grey-literature searches.

atoms.canonical_statement: The authors concluded that adjunctive therapies added to metformin differed in glycemic, weight, blood-pressure, hypoglycemia, and genital-infection effects; no therapy increased urinary-tract-infection risk versus placebo.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: all agents analyzed in our NMA proved effective ... Evaluated agents differed in their effects on BW, SBP, hypoglycemia and GTI; however no medication increased the risk of UTI when compared to placebo.
